questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Communities solving their internet problems
The history of the first internet browsers
Why dial-up internet was better than broadband
How farmers in England grow crops in bad weather
questions.why: Sam says they'll find out how some communities are working together to fix their internet connection problems.

questions.q: What does Sam remember about dial-up internet?
options: It was fast but very expensive to use
It only worked late at night in most homes
It was slow and stopped you using the phone
It made no noise when it was connecting
questions.why: She says it was slow, websites took forever, and you couldn't use the internet and phone together.

questions.q: Why does Katie think her internet in Dorset is unreliable?
options: Because too many people use it at the same time
The cables under the ground are old
Because the weather in Dorset is often stormy
Because her computer is too old to connect properly
questions.why: Katie says most of their underground cabling is very old and needs replacing.

questions.q: Why does Neil mention Katie's problem in Dorset?
options: To show that the UK has the worst internet in Europe
To show that rural life is better without the internet
To explain how fibre optics were first invented
To show that poor internet isn't just a remote-area issue
questions.why: He says you might think only remote places struggle, 'but that's not always true. Even here in the UK'.

questions.q: What is life like in Aamer Hayat's village in Punjab?
options: It is close to a big town with good shops
It has fast internet but no electricity at all
It is far from town and has no phone signal
It has very poor land for growing crops
questions.why: His village is a three-hour drive from the nearest town, and he can't make a phone call, even with 2G.

questions.q: Why is the internet so important to Aamer?
options: He needs weather reports for his crops
He wants to sell his farm to people online
He wants to watch videos about city life
He needs it to talk to his children abroad
questions.why: Neil says knowing when rain is coming can mean his crops succeed or fail.

questions.q: What did the villagers do to solve their problem?
options: They moved to the nearest town to get online
They asked the government to lay new cables
They bought satellite phones for every family
They built a tall tower linking five villages
questions.why: They built their own fifty-metre-high tower, linking a network of five villages to the internet.

questions.q: According to Aamer, how has his way of farming changed?
options: He has stopped farming and now sells gadgets
He now gets reliable information online
He still depends on what his neighbours tell him
He has moved from growing crops to keeping horses
questions.why: He used to rely on word-of-mouth, but now gets information 'right from the horse's mouth' through the internet.
